                                      PROJECT NO. 58777

 TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                            §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                         §                 OF TEXAS
 REGION UNDER § 25.508                            §

           OFFICE OF PUBLIC UTILITY COUNSEL’S POSITION ON
    ERCOT’S FINAL RECOMMENDATION OF MODELING ASSUMPTIONS AND
           CONE STUDY FOR THE 2026 RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT

       The Office of Public Utility Counsel (OPUC) files the following comments in response to

ERCOT’s Final Recommendation of Modeling Assumptions and Cone Study for the 2026

Reliability Assessment filed on March 23, 2026. After speaking with Public Utility Commission

Staff, it was requested that OPUC file the comments on the Interchange to be part of the record.

Pursuant to that request, OPUC now submits these comments.

General Comment:

   •   Reliability assessment is a valuable exercise, but it should avoid overly conservative

       assumptions that bias towards overbuilding.

Concern:

   •   Magnitude of Rotating Outages

       -   OPUC is concerned that ERCOT’s current methodology underestimates the amount of

           load that will be able to be rotated in 2029.

       -   The current 2029 assumption (14.5 gigawatts (GW)) seems too low. OPUC suggests

           that it scale with load growth. A reasonable range for 2029 may be closer to 15-16 GW

           based on general growth.

       -   Rotating outages primarily affect residential customers. Assumptions should reflect

           their expected share of load.




                                                 1
 Matters OPUC supports:

   1) CONE:

      •   OPUC supports ERCOT initiating CONE update by Brattle, as well as their

          recommendations for technologies to consider.

   2) Load forecasting:

      •   OPUC supports ERCOT’s recommendation to use a load forecast based on the 2026

          RTP as well as their proposal to evaluate a range of forecast scenarios.

      •   OPUC suggests that one of the scenarios considered be a low load (no large load)

          scenario (i.e. 2-5% annual growth) to provide a baseline for comparison.

      •   Any assumed large load flexibility/curtailment must be consistently modeled, either as

          reduced demand or as a resource, but not both, nor ignored.

      •   OPUC agrees that observed price responsiveness of certain large loads should be

          incorporated.

   3) Large Load & Flexibility Assumptions:

      •   Assumptions regarding behind-the-meter generation and back-up generation must align

          with statutory requirements of Senate Bill 6.

      •   ERCOT should clearly state document assumptions regarding: (1) installation of back-

          up generation, and (2) curtailment behavior of large loads.

      •   Modeling should reflect how the system will actually behave, including net-metered

          load curtailment, ahead of emergencies.

      •   OPUC eagerly awaits the results of the recent survey of loads before offering specific

          suggestions.




                                               2
 4) Resource Assumptions

   •   OPUC supports ERCOT’s proposal to begin with Capacity, Demand, and Reserves

       (CDR) resources and include projects funded by the Texas Energy Fund where

       applicable.

   •   OPUC is satisfied with ERCOT’s proposals regarding resource outage probabilities.

5) Fuel Price Assumptions

   •   Fuel price uncertainty is less likely to materially affect results compared to capacity

       cost assumptions.

   •   Using a standard forecast, like the EIA fuel forecast, is sufficient and scenario

       expansion should prioritize load forecasts instead.

6) Weather Modeling

   •   OPUC supports modeling a winter season (December – February) as a unified period

       rather than separate months. Alternatively, all three months could be represented with

       similar weather assumptions. In the end, the risk of extreme cold weather should be

       reflected across December, January, and February.

   •   There is value in exploring if the duration of cold weather, rather than just temperature,

       drives outage risk.

7) Zonal Modeling

   •   Given resource and time constraints, the reliability assessment’s focus should remain

       on load forecast scenarios rather than zonal modeling.

8) Reliability Criteria Framework

   •   Reliability assessments must satisfy all three criteria: (1) frequency of events,

       (2) magnitude of load shed, and (3) duration of outages.


                                             3
        •   Current magnitude assumptions may bias results toward overestimating system

           reliability.

   9) Battery Modeling

       •   Consider evaluating standalone battery storage, rather than only solar plus battery

           combinations.

   10) Market Design

       •   Modeling should include real-world mechanisms, such as the Emergency Pricing

           Program, to avoid overstating generator revenues.

       •   Additional sensitivities (i.e. 12CP v. 4CP) could be useful to assess reliability impacts.



Date: April 2, 2026

                                              Respectfully submitted,
                                              Benjamin Barkley
                                              Chief Executive and Public Counsel
                                              State Bar No. 24092083
